oldContent: We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs.rss We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more en-US 60 silverorange: Director of Business Development Anywhere in the World 🇨🇦 Canada Prince Edward Island Sales and Marketing Full-Time <img src="https://we-work-remotely.imgix.net/logos/0171/0794/logo.gif?ixlib=rails-4.0.0&w=50&h=50&dpr=2&fit=fill&auto=compress" /> <p> <strong>Headquarters:</strong> Charlottetown, PE <br /><strong>URL:</strong> <a href="https://www.silverorange.com/">https://www.silverorange.com/</a> </p> <h3><strong><span>The company</span></strong></h3> <div><span>silverorange is a design and development agency based in Canada. We design and develop simple yet powerful web and mobile applications. When pursuing work, we focus on interesting and meaningful projects. Over our 26 years as a company, we've worked with well-known technology organizations like Duolingo and Mozilla, not-for-profit organizations working in areas including </span><a href="https://blog.silverorange.com/usability-for-promotion-codes-and-access-codes"><span>affordable internet access for low-income families</span></a><span>, and with </span><a href="https://www.emrap.org/"><span>world-renowned doctors training other doctors</span></a><span> through online education.</span></div> <div>&nbsp;</div> <div><span>We’re proud of the fantastic products we’ve built in partnership with our clients and we’re actively invested in the processes behind these products. We are committed to fostering a team-focused approach in our work of building great user-focused systems, while also placing a serious emphasis on quality of life, openness, empathy, and a supportive work environment.</span></div> <h3><strong><span>The position</span></strong></h3> <div><span>We're looking for a full-time Director of Business Development to lead our efforts to expand our client base. For a long time silverorange successfully relied on word of mouth and existing partnerships to sustain our growth - we have now reached a point where we feel we need a dedicated business development specialist in order to meet our business goals. We’re looking for a strategic and proactive person who will leverage their expertise to shape our business development strategy and implement the processes to support sustained growth.&nbsp;</span></div> <div>&nbsp;</div> <div><span>This position is available immediately and we will work with you to get you started as soon as possible.</span></div> <h3><strong><span>Responsibilities</span></strong></h3> <ul> <li><span>Develop, maintain, and implement a strategic business development plan.&nbsp;</span></li> <li><span>Build out our sales pipeline; implement and maintain a Customer Relationship Management (CRM) system or alternative for leads.</span></li> <li><span>Seek out, establish, and cultivate new client relationships.</span></li> <li><span>Act as the face of the company for events, client visits, business mixers etc.&nbsp;</span></li> <li><span>Seek and respond to appropriate requests for proposals; create proposals for potential new clients.</span></li> <li><span>Recommend a business-to-business marketing strategy while keeping an eye on industry trends, advise leadership of potential new markets and research to support our services.</span></li> <li><span>Maintain and/or coordinate open communication with existing and former clients to foster future work.</span></li> <li><span>Regularly report to the operations team on business development activities.</span></li> </ul> <h3><strong><span>Requirements</span></strong></h3> <ul> <li><span>Be eligible &amp; available to work from Canada.&nbsp;</span></li> <li><span>Be willing and able to travel nationally and internationally to meet with prospective clients.</span></li> <li><span>5+ years of experience leading business-to-business sales for an organization in the digital services industry.</span></li> <li><span>Experience developing, maintaining, and implementing a business development plan and actively managing a sales pipeline.</span></li> <li><span>Excellent organizational, verbal, and written communication skills. Experience working in a remote or asynchronous environment is an asset.</span></li> <li><span>Strong sense of ownership over and self-direction in the work.</span></li> <li><span>Strong client management skills.</span></li> </ul> <h3><strong><span>Growth &amp; ownership</span></strong></h3> <div><span>Our team is co-operative and will help you learn and expand your skills via mentoring, team-wide support, and learning opportunities. All members of the team are encouraged and given space to grow as individual contributors, and have ongoing opportunities in project and team leadership.</span></div> <div>&nbsp;</div> <div><span>We’re excited to hear your fresh ideas and approach. We have decades of collective experience, and we all continue to become better at what we do by both teaching and learning from each other. Add your voice to our mix!</span></div> <div>&nbsp;</div> <div><span>Opportunity for employee ownership is a fundamental part of silverorange (non-founders currently own more than a third of the company) and we’re currently working on new ways to transfer even more ownership to employees.</span></div> <h3><strong><span>Inclusion &amp; diversity</span></strong></h3> <div><span>People with different backgrounds and experiences make us stronger, and we’re always looking for ways to improve. Our team is getting more diverse across many dimensions of diversity, but we’re still missing perspectives that could make our work better. The post Vercel Releases UI SDK: 50+ UI Behaviors for AI Coding Agents appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Vercel Labs has released UI SDK , an open-source beta library of interface behaviors built for coding agents. Vercel UI SDK is a headless library that ships behaviors, not finished components. Agents combine those behaviors into accessible components for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 50+ behaviors, 51 component modules in the repo, 6 npm packages at 0.1.0-beta.1 Runs on: Any modern browser, no GPU. React 19+, Vue 3.5+, Svelte 5.33+, Solid 2 RC, or plain Web Components Performance: In Vercel’s own test, an agent used 69% fewer tool calls on a settings task Best: Task time fell 61%, from 41 s to 16 s, with the agent bridge (self-reported) Worst: That benchmark covers 1 task and 3 runs, and beta APIs may still change What is Vercel UI SDK? UI SDK is a library of UI behaviors from Vercel Labs that agents assemble into components. The README lists keyboard navigation, focus, selection, dismissal, popups, drag and drop, and the ARIA they need. All of it lives in @ui-sdk/core . Thin adapters render it in each framework. The project site explains the idea with a Select. You do not hand the agent a finished Select. You hand it a popup, a selection model and typeahead. Those same parts can produce an autocomplete, a combobox, or a component nobody has designed yet. How does UI SDK work? Components start as primitives defined with definePrimitive . A primitive declares state, an API and slots. Slots attach attributes, events and behaviors to DOM parts. The README example builds a search field with createFocusRecovery . Its Clear button appears only when there is text. Each framework then renders the primitive with createParts . The README says the parts are the same in all 5 adapters. So 1 behavior definition can serve a React app and a Svelte app. Which behaviors ship? Behaviors shown on ui-sdk.dev include: createRovingFocus : arrow keys move through a list with 1 Tab stop createTypeahead : type a few letters to jump to an item createPopup : opens next to its trigger and stays on screen createSelection : select 1 or many, with Shift and Ctrl createReorder , createResize , createViewport and createVirtualizer The docs group behaviors into 10 categories, from Focus and Keys to Canvas. Prebuilt components include Select, Combobox, Date Picker, Menu, Tree and Color Picker. How do agents learn it? Setup is a prompt you paste into your agent . It installs the packages and adds a note to AGENTS.md . That note points the agent to the ui-sdk skill and to llms.txt inside the package docs. The skill installs with npx skills add vercel-labs/ui --skill ui-sdk . Pages without a build step can load web.js and web.css from ui-sdk.dev, per the skill listing . Can agents operate the UI directly? Yes, the agent docs describe a bridge created with createAgent() before the page renders. agent.snapshot() lists components, their state and available actions. agent.act() runs an action, such as renaming a project with setValue . Apps can pass an allow callback to approve or refuse actions. Change callbacks receive source: "agent" and can cancel the change. Tools can also be registered with supported browsers through WebMCP. UI SDK benchmark: agent bridge vs browser tools Vercel compared its bridge against browser tools on 1 project-settings task. The agent renamed a project, updated members and notification settings, then saved. Both agents used Sonnet through Claude Code, with the same task and system prompt. Figures are medians of 3 runs . Metric Browser tools UI SDK + bridge Change Tool calls 16 5 -69% Text read (characters) 39.8k 6.8k -83% Time 41 s 16 s -61% Cost $0.073 $0.032 -56% Treat these as directional. The sample is 1 task, and the browser-tools run used a different component library. Vercel does not name the Sonnet version. Deployment and availability All 6 packages are on npm at 0.1.0-beta.1 , published November 12, 2026, under Apache-2.0. Install with npm install @ui-sdk/react @ui-sdk/core , swapping the adapter per framework. Peer requirements are strict: React 19+ , Vue 3.5+ , Svelte 5.33+ and Solid 2.0.0-rc.14+ . An optional web.css file gives components a default look. How does UI SDK compare with Radix, React Aria, Base UI and Ark UI? Coding agents compose them into accessible components for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components, with a bridge for direct UI control. The post Vercel Releases UI SDK: 50+ UI Behaviors for AI Coding Agents appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Vercel Labs has released UI SDK , an open-source beta library of interface behaviors built for coding agents. Vercel UI SDK is a headless library that ships behaviors, not finished components. Agents combine those behaviors into accessible components for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 50+ behaviors, 51 component modules in the repo, 6 npm packages at 0.1.0-beta.1 Runs on: Any modern browser, no GPU. React 19+, Vue 3.5+, Svelte 5.33+, Solid 2 RC, or plain Web Components Performance: In Vercel’s own test, an agent used 69% fewer tool calls on a settings task Best: Task time fell 61%, from 41 s to 16 s, with the agent bridge (self-reported) Worst: That benchmark covers 1 task and 3 runs, and beta APIs may still change What is Vercel UI SDK? UI SDK is a library of UI behaviors from Vercel Labs that agents assemble into components. The README lists keyboard navigation, focus, selection, dismissal, popups, drag and drop, and the ARIA they need. All of it lives in @ui-sdk/core . Thin adapters render it in each framework. The project site explains the idea with a Select. You do not hand the agent a finished Select. You hand it a popup, a selection model and typeahead. Those same parts can produce an autocomplete, a combobox, or a component nobody has designed yet. How does UI SDK work? Components start as primitives defined with definePrimitive . A primitive declares state, an API and slots. Slots attach attributes, events and behaviors to DOM parts. The README example builds a search field with createFocusRecovery . Its Clear button appears only when there is text. Each framework then renders the primitive with createParts . The README says the parts are the same in all 5 adapters. So 1 behavior definition can serve a React app and a Svelte app. Which behaviors ship? Behaviors shown on ui-sdk.dev include: createRovingFocus : arrow keys move through a list with 1 Tab stop createTypeahead : type a few letters to jump to an item createPopup : opens next to its trigger and stays on screen createSelection : select 1 or many, with Shift and Ctrl createReorder , createResize , createViewport and createVirtualizer The docs group behaviors into 10 categories, from Focus and Keys to Canvas. Prebuilt components include Select, Combobox, Date Picker, Menu, Tree and Color Picker. How do agents learn it? Setup is a prompt you paste into your agent . It installs the packages and adds a note to AGENTS.md . That note points the agent to the ui-sdk skill and to llms.txt inside the package docs. The skill installs with npx skills add vercel-labs/ui --skill ui-sdk . Pages without a build step can load web.js and web.css from ui-sdk.dev, per the skill listing . Can agents operate the UI directly? Yes, the agent docs describe a bridge created with createAgent() before the page renders. agent.snapshot() lists components, their state and available actions. agent.act() runs an action, such as renaming a project with setValue . Apps can pass an allow callback to approve or refuse actions. Change callbacks receive source: "agent" and can cancel the change. Tools can also be registered with supported browsers through WebMCP. UI SDK benchmark: agent bridge vs browser tools Vercel compared its bridge against browser tools on 1 project-settings task. The agent renamed a project, updated members and notification settings, then saved. Both agents used Sonnet through Claude Code, with the same task and system prompt. Figures are medians of 3 runs . Metric Browser tools UI SDK + bridge Change Tool calls 16 5 -69% Text read (characters) 39.8k 6.8k -83% Time 41 s 16 s -61% Cost $0.073 $0.032 -56% Treat these as directional. The sample is 1 task, and the browser-tools run used a different component library. Vercel does not name the Sonnet version. Deployment and availability All 6 packages are on npm at 0.1.0-beta.1 , published November 12, 2026, under Apache-2.0. Install with npm install @ui-sdk/react @ui-sdk/core , swapping the adapter per framework. Peer requirements are strict: React 19+ , Vue 3.5+ , Svelte 5.33+ and Solid 2.0.0-rc.14+ . An optional web.css file gives components a default look. How does UI SDK compare with Radix, React Aria, Base UI and Ark UI? Metrics UI SDK Radix Primitives React Aria Components Base UI Ark UI Model Behaviors composed by agents Unstyled components Hooks and components Unstyled components Components on Zag.js state machines Frameworks React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, Web Components React React React React, Vue, Solid, Svelte License Apache-2.0 MIT Apache-2.0 MIT MIT Latest npm version 0.1.0-beta.1 1.8.1 1.22.1 1.9.0 5.40.0 React peer range 19+ 16.8 to 19 16.8 to 19 17 to 19 18+ Agent skill and runtime bridge Yes (skill, llms.txt, createAgent, WebMCP) Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Versions and peer ranges are from npm as of November 13, 2026. React Aria hooks and Ark UI’s Zag.js machines already separate behavior from markup. UI SDK’s difference is the agent layer: a skill, bundled llms.txt and a runtime bridge Key Takeaways 50+ behaviors, 1 core, 5 framework adapters. Agents compose components from behaviors, not templates. createAgent lets agents act on UI state without screenshots. Self-reported: 61% faster and 56% cheaper on 1 task. Beta at 0.1.0-beta.1, with React 19 as the minimum. Check out the GitHub repo , docs and npm package . It reaches 84.33% on FactKG using 108x fewer document tokens than full context. The post Stanford Research Open-Sources Memorilla, a Latent Memory Module for Frozen LLMs appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Stanford researchers have released Memorilla , an open-source memory system for LLMs. The Memorilla memory system reads a whole document collection and hands a frozen LLM just 16 memory tokens. On FactKG, a frozen Qwen3-8B scored 84.33% with Memorilla, against 80.43% with every document in context . It did that with 108x fewer document tokens. Code, training recipes and checkpoints are public under Apache 2.0 . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 194M-parameter trainable memory module. It always outputs 16 memory tokens, whatever the collection size. The encoder ( Qwen3-Embedding-4B ) and decoder ( Qwen3-8B ) stay frozen. Runs on: Linux with CUDA GPUs and Python 3.11. The quickstart needs 1 GPU with 80 GB (recipes ran on H100 80GB). No quantized variants disclosed. Performance: Highest reported average across 8 benchmarks (49.68), top score on 5 of 8. Best: PersonaMem-v2 accuracy of 44.60%, versus 27.92% for full context. Worst: PubMedQA accuracy of 59.00%, versus 69.00% for LLMLingua-2. What is Memorilla? Memorilla is a memory module that turns a document collection into 16 vectors for a frozen LLM. The work comes from Jure Leskovec’s SNAP group, with co-authors from Toronto, Penn and MIT. A frozen LLM can only use what sits in its context window. Full-context prompting grows slower as history grows. Retrieval pastes the chunks most similar to the question, and can miss weaker clues. Memorilla takes a third route: it learns what each question needs from the whole store. How does Memorilla work? The pipeline has 3 steps: Encode once. A frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B embeds each document a single time. New documents never force re-encoding of old ones. Read per question. 16 learned slots attend to the question and the full store. The module uses 2 cross-attention layers with 8 heads. Inject. The slots are projected into Qwen3-8B’s input embedding space and prepended to the question. Only the memory module trains: 194,123,776 parameters for the 8B decoder. Training runs in 3 stages. Stage 1 uses about 1.98M Wikipedia paraphrase-reconstruction examples. Stage 2 adds about 1.34M examples from 10 QA and summarization datasets. Stage 3 fine-tunes on all 8 benchmarks. The full recipe takes about 19 hours on 4 H100 GPUs. How does Memorilla perform on benchmarks? All baselines use the same frozen Qwen3-8B, per the paper’s main table. Scores are self-reported by the research team. FactKG: 84.33% accuracy, versus 80.43% full context and 80.38% MemoRAG. PersonaMem-v2: 44.60%, versus 30.90% for xRAG, the next best method. TriviaQA: 57.00 exact match, just ahead of MemoRAG at 56.60. LaMP-4 / LaMP-7: 18.15 and 48.37 ROUGE-L, both the best scores. Average: 49.68, versus 41.92 for xRAG, 40.75 for LLMLingua-2 and 38.02 for Mem0. Memorilla loses on 3 benchmarks. On PubMedQA it scores 59.00%, while LLMLingua-2 reaches 69.00%. Those abstracts total only 324 tokens, so compression has little to gain. MemoRAG leads on PersonalizationV4 (67.88% vs 66.65%) and NarrativeQA ROUGE-L (20.51 vs 19.31). MemoRAG used about 690x and 50x more document tokens there. Compression peaks on NarrativeQA: 16 tokens replace 67,385 document tokens, a 4,212x cut. As agent memory, 8 memory tokens lift a Qwen3-4B TextWorld agent from 18.6% to 24.2% average success. How fast is Memorilla compared to full context? On 1 H100, Memorilla answers in 0.74 s at 512 documents (about 128K tokens). Full context slows from 0.75 s to 19.9 s, which is 27x slower. The memory module itself takes about 2 ms. An optional memory cache precomputes cross-attention keys and values. On 1 B200, a question then takes 8.1 ms at 1M documents and 33 ms at 4M. With torch.compile , the 1M case drops to 5.0 ms. The cache costs 80 GiB at 4M documents. How do you run Memorilla? Install with uv on Linux, then load MemoryVLLM.from_pretrained . The first run downloads about 25 GB of models. Checkpoints live at memorilla/Memorilla-Qwen3-8B as Stage 1, 2, 3, PV4 and PMv2 folders. Each checkpoint must run with the decoder it was trained with ( evaluation docs ). Custom data needs parquet files with collection_id , question , answer and documents columns. The research team also released PersonalizationV4 : 149 synthetic users, 200 conversations each, under CC BY 4.0. Memorilla vs Mem0, MemoRAG and xRAG Benchmark scores come from Memorilla’s paper, which ran every baseline on the same Qwen3-8B. Licenses come from each project’s repository. FactKG: 84.33% vs 80.43% full context, with 108x fewer tokens. Highest reported 8-benchmark average: 49.68. Weak spot: PubMedQA at 59.00% and fine-grained facts. It reaches 84.33% on FactKG using 108x fewer document tokens than full context. The post Stanford Research Open-Sources Memorilla, a Latent Memory Module for Frozen LLMs appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Stanford researchers have released Memorilla , an open-source memory system for LLMs. The Memorilla memory system reads a whole document collection and hands a frozen LLM just 16 memory tokens. On FactKG, a frozen Qwen3-8B scored 84.33% with Memorilla, against 80.43% with every document in context . It did that with 108x fewer document tokens. Code, training recipes and checkpoints are public under Apache 2.0 . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 194M-parameter trainable memory module. It always outputs 16 memory tokens, whatever the collection size. The encoder ( Qwen3-Embedding-4B ) and decoder ( Qwen3-8B ) stay frozen. Runs on: Linux with CUDA GPUs and Python 3.11. The quickstart needs 1 GPU with 80 GB (recipes ran on H100 80GB). No quantized variants disclosed. Performance: Highest reported average across 8 benchmarks (49.68), top score on 5 of 8. Best: PersonaMem-v2 accuracy of 44.60%, versus 27.92% for full context. Worst: PubMedQA accuracy of 59.00%, versus 69.00% for LLMLingua-2. What is Memorilla? Memorilla is a memory module that turns a document collection into 16 vectors for a frozen LLM. The work comes from Jure Leskovec’s SNAP group, with co-authors from Toronto, Penn and MIT. A frozen LLM can only use what sits in its context window. Full-context prompting grows slower as history grows. Retrieval pastes the chunks most similar to the question, and can miss weaker clues. Memorilla takes a third route: it learns what each question needs from the whole store. How does Memorilla work? The pipeline has 3 steps: Encode once. A frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B embeds each document a single time. New documents never force re-encoding of old ones. Read per question. 16 learned slots attend to the question and the full store. The module uses 2 cross-attention layers with 8 heads. Inject. The slots are projected into Qwen3-8B’s input embedding space and prepended to the question. Only the memory module trains: 194,123,776 parameters for the 8B decoder. Training runs in 3 stages. Stage 1 uses about 1.98M Wikipedia paraphrase-reconstruction examples. Stage 2 adds about 1.34M examples from 10 QA and summarization datasets. Stage 3 fine-tunes on all 8 benchmarks. The full recipe takes about 19 hours on 4 H100 GPUs. How does Memorilla perform on benchmarks? All baselines use the same frozen Qwen3-8B, per the paper’s main table. Scores are self-reported by the research team. FactKG: 84.33% accuracy, versus 80.43% full context and 80.38% MemoRAG. PersonaMem-v2: 44.60%, versus 30.90% for xRAG, the next best method. TriviaQA: 57.00 exact match, just ahead of MemoRAG at 56.60. LaMP-4 / LaMP-7: 18.15 and 48.37 ROUGE-L, both the best scores. Average: 49.68, versus 41.92 for xRAG, 40.75 for LLMLingua-2 and 38.02 for Mem0. Memorilla loses on 3 benchmarks. On PubMedQA it scores 59.00%, while LLMLingua-2 reaches 69.00%. Those abstracts total only 324 tokens, so compression has little to gain. MemoRAG leads on PersonalizationV4 (67.88% vs 66.65%) and NarrativeQA ROUGE-L (20.51 vs 19.31). MemoRAG used about 690x and 50x more document tokens there. Compression peaks on NarrativeQA: 16 tokens replace 67,385 document tokens, a 4,212x cut. As agent memory, 8 memory tokens lift a Qwen3-4B TextWorld agent from 18.6% to 24.2% average success. How fast is Memorilla compared to full context? On 1 H100, Memorilla answers in 0.74 s at 512 documents (about 128K tokens). Full context slows from 0.75 s to 19.9 s, which is 27x slower. The memory module itself takes about 2 ms. An optional memory cache precomputes cross-attention keys and values. On 1 B200, a question then takes 8.1 ms at 1M documents and 33 ms at 4M. With torch.compile , the 1M case drops to 5.0 ms. The cache costs 80 GiB at 4M documents. How do you run Memorilla? Install with uv on Linux, then load MemoryVLLM.from_pretrained . The first run downloads about 25 GB of models. Checkpoints live at memorilla/Memorilla-Qwen3-8B as Stage 1, 2, 3, PV4 and PMv2 folders. Each checkpoint must run with the decoder it was trained with ( evaluation docs ). Custom data needs parquet files with collection_id , question , answer and documents columns. The research team also released PersonalizationV4 : 149 synthetic users, 200 conversations each, under CC BY 4.0. Memorilla vs Mem0, MemoRAG and xRAG Benchmark scores come from Memorilla’s paper, which ran every baseline on the same Qwen3-8B. Licenses come from each project’s repository. FactKG: 84.33% vs 80.43% full context, with 108x fewer tokens. Highest reported 8-benchmark average: 49.68. Weak spot: PubMedQA at 59.00% and fine-grained facts. A frontier LLM reads a small model’s weights, edits them in a sandbox, and tests each change, with no gradients and about $5 to $10 per run. The post Cmpnd Releases dspy-wsp: Weight-Space Programming Comes to DSPy appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Cmpnd has released dspy-wsp , a prototype optimizer that brings weight-space programming to DSPy . Weight-space programming is a technique in which a frontier LLM reads another model’s weights and edits them directly. There are no gradients, no training loop and no fine-tuning dataset. dspy-wsp packages this as WeightSpace , an optimizer that plugs into any DSPy program and metric. In Cmpnd’s tests, about $5 to $10 of GPT-6-Astra calls improved every decision model they tried. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR What it is: A DSPy optimizer ( WeightSpace ) where a writer LLM edits a student model’s weights. MIT license, pip install dspy-wsp , needs DSPy 3.5. Size: Tested on open decision models from 0.6B to 9B parameters. One 25-pass run edited a single layer or head. Runs on: One Mac for all experiments. 2B models used about 6 GB of memory. d1-omni-600M needs 4 GB or more (Mac or GPU). Performance: WeightSpace alone added 1.9 to 16.1 points on Typed Decisions. With ReAnchor, gains were 6.5 to 20.0 points. Best: d1-omni-600M rose from 50.9% to 69.1% (+18.3) with WeightSpace + ReAnchor. Worst: Clef-Flash (9B) gained only +1.9 from WeightSpace alone. With the original paper’s stricter rule, d1-omni-600M gained just +2.8. Bottom line: Best: a cheap, gradient-free edit that ships as a small, verifiable patch. Worst: very experimental, slow (78 to 167 minutes per run) and weakest on larger models. What is weight-space programming? Weight-space programming (WSP) treats a neural network’s weights as a program that can be read and rewritten. The idea comes from MIT research: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming . A frontier model (the research team used GPT-6-Astra) looks at weight tensors, reasons about what each part computes, and changes them to match a goal written in plain English. The research team stresses that WSP names an emerging capability, not a fixed method. Gradients were banned in their experiments, but the concept does not rule them out. How is it different from fine-tuning or prompt optimization? It helps to compare the 3 levers developers usually pull: Prompt optimization (DSPy’s MIPROv2, GEPA ) edits text: instructions and examples. The model’s weights never change. Fine-tuning (DSPy’s BootstrapFinetune, used inside BetterTogether ) changes weights with gradient descent. It needs training data, a training loop and usually a GPU. Weight-space programming changes weights by reasoning. The editor forms a hypothesis (“these neurons over-score option B”), writes code to patch them, and checks the result with a few forward passes. The research post frames WSP as the next step after using LLMs to optimize text artifacts. Earlier work let LLMs hill-climb on prompts, harnesses and training code. Weights were left to Adam or to trained weight-generating networks. WSP argues LLM reasoning can now reach the weights directly. What did the original research show? The MIT team ran 9 experiments. Several are striking: Reading weights: Astra named the correct game (Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, Freeway) for 4 PPO policy networks from weights alone. Fixing a broken policy: A Kinetix car-on-ramp policy failed all 256 episodes. One edit to 3.5% of its weights made it succeed in all 1,024 test episodes. Writing from zero: On MinAtar Breakout, a zero-initialized network written in 1 shot scored 517.4. PPO reached 25.3 after 500M steps. Fixing an LLM: Qwen3.5-0.8B looped on math problems. Astra traced the issue to MLP layers 15 and 19 and changed 131,072 weights (0.016% of the model). With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The research also shows limits. On Gemma 3 270M, edits moved MATH-500 from 6.8% to between 7.0% and 7.7%. The research team did not count that as a real gain. Editing can remove an obstacle, but it could not add a missing ability. How does dspy-wsp work? dspy-wsp turns that research loop into a standard DSPy optimizer. The GitHub Repo describes 3 actors: The student: the small model your DSPy program runs on. Its weights load into a local Python process. The writer: a frontier LLM, recommended as gpt-6-astra at maximum reasoning effort. The sandbox: a kernel where the writer runs code. macOS uses built-in sandbox-exec ; Linux uses bubblewrap. The writer works in turns. Each turn has a short explanation, then 1 code block. That block is either: a Python block that reads or edits weights inside the sandbox, or a forward block that runs your DSPy program on practice examples. Forward passes come from a fixed budget ( max_passes=25 in the tests). When the budget runs out, the writer’s best edit becomes the patch. A hidden validation set then compares original and edited weights on the same examples and seeds. What data does the writer see? The repo is explicit about data separation: trainset is the writer’s practice set. holdout moves a fraction (0.25 in the example) of training data into a check set. The writer can score edits on it but never sees the examples. valset stays hidden and runs once at the end. Metrics can return dspy.Prediction(score=..., feedback=...) . The feedback text is visible to the writer. What did the writer actually change? The results write-up lists every edit. The edits are small and targeted: Model Tensor edited Scope Time Writer cost d1-omni-600M head.scorer.1.weight (+ bias, scorer.3.weight ) 112,640 of 1,048,576 entries, plus 220 78 min $7.63 NanoJev (Qwen3-0.6B) scalar.weight 1,024 entries 167 min $6.92 d1-2B layers.23.feed_forward.w2.weight All 15.7M entries, rank-9 change 83 min $5.42 d1-2B has no decision head, so the writer edited its backbone at layer 23. On d1-omni-600M, the writer rewrote part of the decision head’s scorer. What does the code look like? The Repo example triages support tickets. The signature uses only decision-type outputs: Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser import dspy from typing import Literal from dspy_wsp import WeightSpace, load_decision_backend class Triage(dspy.Signature): """Triage a support ticket.""" ticket: str = dspy.InputField() urgent: bool = dspy.OutputField(desc="Does this ticket need a reply today?") team: Literal["billing", "technical", "account"] = dspy.OutputField(desc="Which team should handle it?") backend = load_decision_backend("d1") # d1-omni-600M optimizer = WeightSpace( metric=metric, writer_lm=dspy.LM("openai/gpt-6-astra", model_type="responses", reasoning_effort="max"), backend=backend, max_passes=25, holdout=0.25, run_dir="runs/triage", ) compiled = optimizer.compile(dspy.Predict(Triage), trainset=train, valset=test) compiled(ticket="I was charged twice this month.") # runs on the edited weights After compile , the program calls the edited local model instead of a hosted API. compiled.wsp_patch.summary() shows what changed. We’ve already rounded up some of the best early Black Friday deals we’ve come across, but if you’re looking to save on outdoor gear or pick up something for an upcoming trip, REI’s annual Holiday Sale , which runs through November 23rd, is worth checking out. As usual, the outdoor retailer is offering discounts on everything from smartwatches to camping equipment. In some cases, we’re seeing some of the lowest prices we’ve seen on our favorite wearables, including Garmin’s Forerunner 570 , while gadgets like the InReach Mini 3 are also receiving sizable discounts. REI members can also use promo code HOLIDAY2026 to save 20 percent on one full-price item, plus an additional 20 percent on one REI Outlet item. To save you time, we’ve sifted through the deluge of discounts to find an assortment of deals we recommend here at The Verge . We’ve also noted when competing retailers are offering lower prices on the same items, so you can be sure you’re getting the best deal possible. Smartwatches and fitness tech Garmin Forerunner 570 Garmin’s Forerunner 570 features a bright OLED display, skin temperature sensors, and a built-in speaker and microphone for taking calls. It also offers multiband GPS, personalized training plans, and up to 11 days of battery life. Where to Buy: $549.99 $449.99 at Amazon $549.99 $449.99 at Best Buy $550 $449.99 at REI Garmin Venu 4 Garmin’s Venu 4 is geared toward the average athlete, offering heart rate alerts, detailed sleep insights, guided meditation, and a wheelchair mode. It also introduces caffeine and alcohol tracking, along with Garmin Coach, which tailors workouts to your fitness history, sleep, and recovery. Where to Buy: $549.93 at Amazon $549.99 at Best Buy $550 $449.99 at REI REI , Amazon , and Best Buy are also selling the Garmin Lily 2 Active for $249.99 ($50 off), which is its lowest price to date. The stylish smartwatch is a great budget-friendly Garmin, especially for people with smaller wrists. Like the standard Lily 2, it offers basic fitness tracking, notifications, and up to five days of battery life; however, the so-called “Active” model adds a physical button, built-in GPS, and support for more sports tracking. Read our Lily 2 review . The Garmin Vivoactive 6 has returned to its all-time low of $249.99 ($50 off) at Amazon , Walmart , and REI . The fitness watch offers up to 11 days of battery life and tracks a range of workouts, including walking, running, cycling, HIIT, golf, and more. It also provides extensive health monitoring, including wrist-based heart rate detection, menstrual cycle and pregnancy tracking, and a customizable morning report that summarizes helpful health-related info. However, it lacks ECG compatibility, though it does have a slightly slimmer profile than its predecessor. Garmin Fenix 8 The Garmin Fenix 8 is a premium multisport watch that features a speaker, mic, and on-device assistant for calls, timers, and voice commands. It also offers elite battery life, dual-frequency GPS, and robust sensors. Read our review . Where to Buy: $999.99 $749.99 at Amazon (43mm) $1099.99 $749.99 at Walmart (47mm) $1099.99 $849.99 at REI (47mm) The Wahoo Kickr V6 Smart Trainer is on sale at REI for $679.99 ($170 off). Like the more affordable Kickr Core 2 we covered in July , the Kickr V6 turns your existing bike into an indoor exercise bike, with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connectivity for pairing with apps like Zwift . However, the higher-end trainer offers up to 2,200W of resistance and can replicate inclines of up to 20 percent, compared to the Core 2’s 1,800W and 16 percent. It also provides more accurate power measurements and is designed so that indoor rides feel more natural. Phone accessories and entertainment EcoFlow Rapid Magnetic Power Bank EcoFlow’s Rapid Magnetic Power Bank is a 10,000mAh Qi2 battery that can snap to the back of your device if you’re using a newer iPhone or select Android devices, thus supplying it with up to 15W of power. It also includes a built-in USB-C cable that can provide up to 65W of power to larger devices, including a 13-inch MacBook Air. Where to Buy: $90 $66.93 at REI If you own an older iPhone with a Lightning port, you can grab InfinityLab’s InstantGo 10,000 Power Bank   for  $41.93 (about $28 off) at REI . The portable battery features a 10,000mAh capacity and a built-in Lightning cable, making it a solid all-in-one option for days when you won’t be near an outlet. It also supports passthrough charging, so you can charge your phone and the power bank at the same time. DJI’s Osmo Mobile 8 is on sale for around $128.99 ($21 off) at REI , Amazon , and Best Buy , which is $10 shy of its best price to date. The smartphone gimbal supports 360-degree horizontal rotation and Apple’s DockKit, which allows the gimbal to track and follow pets and people across a wider range of camera apps. This discounted Advanced Tracking Combo also includes a multifunctional module for tracking people and pets, as well as a built-in tripod and extension rod that make it easier to film yourself without someone behind the camera. Soundcore Liberty 5 The Soundcore Liberty 5 feature adaptive noise cancellation and support for Dolby Audio, along with six swappable tips so you can find the right fit. They also sport an IP55 rating for water and dust resistance and can last up to 48 hours with the included charging case. Where to Buy: $129.99 $89.99 at Amazon $129.99 $89.99 at Walmart $130 $89.99 at REI You can buy Soundcore’s AeroFit 2 for $79.99 ($20 off) at REI , Amazon , and Best Buy , which is $2 shy of their lowest price to date. Their open-ear design lets you listen to music while staying vigilant in your surroundings; they also feature adjustable ear hooks for a secure fit, IP55 water and dust resistance, and up to 42 hours of battery life with the included charging case. Anker Nebula P1 projector Anker’s Nebula P1 is a portable 1080p projector with built-in Google TV and two detachable Bluetooth speakers that deliver better sound than many all-in-one portable projectors. It offers 650 ANSI lumens of brightness and can project images up to 180 inches, while the speakers last up to 20 hours on a charge. Where to Buy: $799 $599.99 at Amazon $799 $599 at Soundcore $799 $699.99 at REI Communication and safety gear Garmin InReach Mini 3 Plus The Mini 3 Plus is identical to the standard model in that it allows you to stay connected while off the grid; however, it also features an audible siren and the ability to send photos and voice messages, in addition to standard texts. Where to Buy: $499.99 $399.99 at Amazon $499.99 $399.99 at REI $499.99 $399.99 at Garmin Garmin’s base InReach Mini 3 is available from REI , Amazon , and Garmin for around $349 ($100 off), nearly matching its lowest price to date. Like the Mini 2, the rugged, palm-sized satellite communicator lets you send texts, share your location, check the weather, and trigger SOS alerts when you’re off the grid, all while offering battery life that can outlast your average smartphone. Unlike the prior version, though, it features a color touchscreen, which makes it easier to navigate menus and bang out messages. Garmin’s InReach Messenger Plus is also on sale at REI , Amazon , and direct from Garmin for $299.99 ($100 off), matching its best price to date. Th
